LPZh9BOjkQs.q: During pre-training, what does backpropagation do after the model predicts the last word of an example?
options: It deletes the example so the model never sees it again
It tweaks all parameters so the true last word becomes a little more likely
It sets a few parameters by hand to match the correct word
It stores the whole example word for word so the model can copy it back out later
LPZh9BOjkQs.why: The model's guess is compared with the true last word, and backpropagation nudges every parameter to make that true word slightly more likely and the others less likely.

LPZh9BOjkQs.q: What does the attention operation in a transformer do?
options: It lets the word vectors share context so each refines its meaning, all in parallel
It reads the text one word at a time from start to finish
It picks the single most likely next word with certainty
It stores extra facts learned during training in a separate memory the model looks up
LPZh9BOjkQs.why: Attention lets the lists of numbers talk to one another and refine their meaning based on context, like turning bank into river bank, and it runs in parallel.

zjkBMFhNj_g.q: Why does he call the trained parameters a lossy compression of the internet?
options: They store an exact copy of every training web page, just packed into a smaller file
They capture the gist of the training text but cannot reproduce it exactly
They are compressed with the same lossless method a zip file uses, so nothing is lost
They keep only the most recent websites crawled and throw away the older pages
zjkBMFhNj_g.why: Roughly 10 TB of text becomes about 140 GB of parameters. Unlike a lossless zip file, the model keeps a gestalt of the text, not an identical copy.

zjkBMFhNj_g.q: Why did the model's dreamed Amazon page contain an ISBN that almost certainly does not exist?
options: The model looked the book up on the internet and copied an ISBN from a page with an error
The training data contained that exact fake ISBN on an Amazon page the model memorized
The model mimics the form of its training documents and fills in plausible looking text
The ISBN was added later during fine-tuning, when labelers wrote example product pages
zjkBMFhNj_g.why: The network knows a number of roughly that length follows ISBN, so it puts in whatever looks reasonable. It is dreaming text from its training distribution, which is hallucination.

zjkBMFhNj_g.q: What changes between pre-training and fine-tuning?
options: The data changes to high quality Q&A conversations, while the next word objective stays the same
The objective changes from next word prediction to classification, while the internet data stays the same
Fine-tuning uses far more text than pre-training, gathered from a much larger internet crawl
Fine-tuning swaps the Transformer for a different architecture built for conversations
zjkBMFhNj_g.why: The optimization stays identical, still next word prediction. Only the data set is swapped for fewer but higher quality conversations written by labelers, which turns the base model into an assistant.

zjkBMFhNj_g.q: Why does the optional third stage use comparison labels?
options: Comparisons are cheaper to store than full answers, so the labeled data set stays much smaller
It is often easier for a labeler to pick the better of several candidate answers than to write one
Comparisons remove the need for a pre-trained base model, so training can start from scratch
Comparisons let the model train without any human input once the first few labels are written
zjkBMFhNj_g.why: Writing a good haiku may be hard, but judging which of a few generated haikus is best is easy. Stage three, RLHF, uses those comparisons to further tune the model.

zjkBMFhNj_g.q: According to the scaling laws, what reliably improves next word prediction accuracy?
options: A new algorithmic breakthrough every year
Training on only high quality fine-tuning data
Reducing the number of parameters N so the model avoids overfitting
Training a bigger model, more parameters N, on more text D
zjkBMFhNj_g.why: Accuracy is a smooth, predictable function of N and D, with no sign of topping out. Algorithmic progress is a bonus, but scale alone offers a dependable path.

zjkBMFhNj_g.q: What does it mean that current language models only have System 1 thinking?
options: They can only answer math questions that follow one fixed pattern, not open ended word problems
They produce each word in one quick instinctive step, without reasoning through possibilities
They need a human to check every answer before the reply is shown to the user
They work in only one language at a time and must translate everything else first
zjkBMFhNj_g.why: The model just goes chunk, chunk, chunk, sampling words in sequence with roughly equal time per word. The goal of System 2 is to convert extra thinking time into accuracy.

zjkBMFhNj_g.q: Why did the Base64 encoded question get past Claude's refusal?
options: Base64 text is filtered out before it reaches the safety check, so only the model sees it
The model cannot actually read Base64, so it guessed an answer without knowing the request
Its refusal training data was mostly English, so it learned to refuse mainly in English
Base64 queries are routed to a different, older model that never had any safety training
zjkBMFhNj_g.why: The model is fluent in Base64 like other languages, but the refusal examples were mostly English. It never correctly learned to refuse the same request in other encodings.

zjkBMFhNj_g.q: How did the fraud link end up in Bing's answer about the best movies of 2022?
options: A web page Bing retrieved held hidden text that the model treated as new instructions
The user typed the link into the prompt by mistake, and Bing repeated it as a source
The model was poisoned during pre-training with a trigger phrase about movie lists
Bing's search ranking promoted a fraudulent movie site to the top of the results
zjkBMFhNj_g.why: This is prompt injection. One retrieved page contained text, often white on white, that hijacked the model and told it to publish the link.

7xTGNNLPyMI.q: Why do LLMs use byte pair encoding instead of feeding in raw bits or bytes?
options: It removes rare words the model should not learn, so the vocabulary stays clean
It shortens the sequence by adding more symbols, since sequence length is precious
It encrypts the text so the model cannot memorize private data word for word
It maps text to dictionary words so each token carries its meaning directly
7xTGNNLPyMI.why: Byte pair encoding merges common pairs into new symbols, trading a bigger vocabulary for shorter sequences. Sequence length is a finite, precious resource for the network.

7xTGNNLPyMI.q: Why doesn't the base model simply answer 4 when you type "What is 2 plus 2" into it?
options: It was trained only on text without numbers, so it has never seen any arithmetic
Its safety training blocks direct answers until the question is phrased as a chat
It needs an internet search tool for any math question, and the base model has none
It is a token autocomplete that continues text like web pages, not an assistant
7xTGNNLPyMI.why: A base model only predicts the next token based on internet documents. The question is just a prefix to continue, so it may wander off instead of answering.

7xTGNNLPyMI.q: How does post-training turn a base model into an assistant?
options: It keeps training the model on example conversations written by human labelers
Programmers write explicit code rules for each kind of question
It retrains the model from scratch on a larger internet crawl filtered for helpful answers
It attaches a search engine that writes the answers
7xTGNNLPyMI.why: The internet dataset is swapped for a dataset of conversations, and training continues with the same algorithm. The model learns to imitate how labelers respond.

7xTGNNLPyMI.q: How did Meta reduce hallucinations in Llama 3?
options: They removed every rare name from the pre-training data so the model could not invent facts
They told the model in its system prompt to always search the web before answering
They probed which facts the model got wrong and trained it to say "I don't know" for those
They had humans rewrite every training answer to sound less confident about facts
7xTGNNLPyMI.why: They quizzed the model on facts, checked its answers, and for questions it got wrong added training examples where the right answer is that it doesn't know. This links its internal uncertainty to saying so.

7xTGNNLPyMI.q: Why is a training answer that states "$3" first and explains afterward a bad example?
options: It uses more tokens than needed, which slows the model and wastes its context window
It forces the model to compute the whole answer in one token, which has limited computation
Readers prefer to see the reasoning first, so labelers are told to always put the answer last
The dollar sign confuses the tokenizer and splits the number into too many pieces
7xTGNNLPyMI.why: Each token gets only a fixed, small amount of computation. Stating the answer first crams all the work into one token, and the explanation after it is just justification.

7xTGNNLPyMI.q: In reinforcement learning on math problems, where do the solutions the model trains on come from?
options: Expert human labelers write one ideal solution for each problem, and the model imitates it
They are copied from textbook answer keys that show every step of the worked solution
A larger teacher model writes them, and the smaller model is trained to imitate each of its steps
The model samples many of its own attempts, and ones reaching the right answer are reinforced
7xTGNNLPyMI.why: Reinforcement learning is guess and check. The model tries many solutions, and the token sequences that reach the correct answer are made more likely.

7xTGNNLPyMI.q: Why could AlphaGo trained with reinforcement learning beat top human players?
options: It learned moves that lead to wins by playing itself, not just by imitating experts
It memorized more expert games than any human could see, then copied the best moves
Go champions wrote a hand-coded strategy for it that covered every opening and endgame
It searched a database of every possible board position to find the winning move
7xTGNNLPyMI.why: Imitating human experts tops out near human level. Reinforcement learning rewards whatever moves actually win, so it can find moves like move 37 that no human would play.

7xTGNNLPyMI.q: Why can't RLHF be run for a very long time the way RL on math problems can?
options: Human labelers get tired of ranking jokes, so the comparison data runs out after a short while
The model runs out of new prompts to practice on after a few thousand updates
The reward model is a neural net that RL learns to game with nonsense that scores high
Longer training always makes the replies too long, and users stop reading them
7xTGNNLPyMI.why: RLHF optimizes against a reward model that only simulates human judgment. Run long enough, RL finds adversarial inputs, like "the the the", that the reward model scores highly.

EWvNQjAaOHw.q: Why does a chat model like GPT-4o have a knowledge cutoff?
options: Post-training deletes any facts learned after a set date to keep the model consistent
Pre-training is costly and rare, so its knowledge stops when it was pre-trained
The context window can only hold information from the years before the model shipped
The company blocks recent facts on purpose to keep the answers safe and checked
EWvNQjAaOHw.why: Pre-training costs tens of millions of dollars and takes months, so it happens infrequently. The model only knows the internet up to when it was pre-trained.

EWvNQjAaOHw.q: When is it worth switching to a thinking model?
options: For simple questions like travel ideas, to get a more polished and complete list
Whenever you want the fastest possible reply
For hard math or coding problems where a fast model's answer falls short
Whenever the question is about recent news events
EWvNQjAaOHw.why: Thinking models were tuned with reinforcement learning and spend extra tokens reasoning, which raises accuracy on hard math and code. For simple questions the wait is not worth it.

EWvNQjAaOHw.q: Why couldn't the model know the White Lotus season 3 release schedule without search?
options: The schedule was set after the model was trained, so it is not in its parameters
TV schedules are filtered out of training data on purpose to avoid spoilers
The model's context window is too small to hold a full season's release schedule
The model is trained to refuse questions about TV shows and other entertainment
EWvNQjAaOHw.why: The schedule was decided recently, after pre-training. Search pulls the web pages into the context window, the model's working memory, so it can answer.

EWvNQjAaOHw.q: What most likely happens when you upload a PDF to an LLM like Claude?
options: The model retrains its parameters on the PDF
The PDF is saved to a memory that every future chat can see
Only the images are analyzed and the text is skipped
It is turned into text and loaded into the context window
EWvNQjAaOHw.why: The PDF is likely converted to text and placed in the token window. Once there, it is in working memory and the model can answer questions about it.

EWvNQjAaOHw.q: Why did Grok 3 get the large multiplication slightly wrong?
options: It wrote Python to do the math, but that code had a small bug
It had no code tool, so it did the math in its head and hallucinated
Its knowledge cutoff predates the numbers, so it guessed from old data
It misread the numbers because the tokenizer split them oddly
EWvNQjAaOHw.why: Without a Python interpreter the model just does its best in its head. It got remarkably close but still hallucinated part of the result.

EWvNQjAaOHw.q: What makes advanced voice mode "true audio" instead of "fake audio"?
options: It uses a more accurate speech-to-text model
It reads its text replies aloud with a much better and more natural sounding voice
The model itself takes in and predicts audio tokens, with no text step
It records your voice and sends it to a human reviewer
EWvNQjAaOHw.why: In true audio, audio is chopped into tokens and handled natively by the language model. Fake audio just converts speech to text and text back to speech around a text model.

EWvNQjAaOHw.q: How can a language model work with images?
options: A separate camera model describes each image in words first, then passes the text on
Every pixel becomes its own word in the vocabulary
The image is compressed into a single special token
The image is cut into patches, each mapped to a token from a vocabulary
EWvNQjAaOHw.why: Images are split into a grid of patches, and each patch is quantized to the closest entry in a patch vocabulary. The transformer then just models a stream of tokens.

EWvNQjAaOHw.q: How does ChatGPT's memory feature carry information between chats?
options: It keeps the full context window from every past chat
It saves short text notes about you and adds them to the start of each conversation
It retrains the model's parameters on your conversations each night so it learns about you
It searches your old chats on the web before answering
EWvNQjAaOHw.why: Memory is a small database of text strings about you. Those strings are prepended to new conversations so the model can see them in its context window.

aircAruvnKk.q: What is the hope for what the hidden layers do when recognizing a 9?
options: Each hidden neuron memorizes one complete training image and fires when it sees that 9
The second layer detects small edges and the third detects parts like loops and lines
The second layer sorts pixels from brightest to darkest and the third counts the dark ones
The hidden layers copy the input pixels forward so the output layer can compare them
aircAruvnKk.why: The layered structure is meant to build up abstraction: edges combine into subcomponents like an upper loop and a vertical line, which combine into a digit.

aircAruvnKk.q: What does a neuron's bias control?
options: Which pixel pattern the neuron picks up on in the layer of neurons that feeds into it
How many neurons in the next layer receive a signal from this neuron
How high the weighted sum must be before the neuron becomes meaningfully active
Whether the neuron squishes its weighted sum with a sigmoid or with ReLU
aircAruvnKk.why: The weights set what pattern the neuron detects. The bias, such as minus 10, is added before the sigmoid and sets the threshold for activity.

aircAruvnKk.q: In the end, what is the whole network, viewed mathematically?
options: A lookup table that stores one answer for each possible image it could be shown
A set of fixed rules written by hand for each digit
A random process that guesses digits until one is right
A single function that takes 784 numbers in and gives 10 numbers out
aircAruvnKk.why: Each neuron is really a function of the previous layer, so the whole network is one complicated function with about 13,000 weights and biases.

IHZwWFHWa-w.q: When is the cost for a single training example small?
options: When the network confidently classifies the image correctly
When all ten output neurons have the same middling activation
When the weights and biases are set randomly
When the output layer has many bright neurons
IHZwWFHWa-w.why: The cost adds up the squared differences between the outputs and the desired values, so it is small only when the output matches the right answer closely.

IHZwWFHWa-w.q: Why do artificial neurons use continuously ranging activations instead of simple on/off values?
options: Because biological neurons fire at many levels, and the network copies them exactly
So the network can store more training images inside each neuron's activation
So the cost function is smooth and can be minimized by small steps downhill
So the output layer can show more than ten digits by mixing its brightness levels
IHZwWFHWa-w.why: Gradient descent needs a smooth cost function so that small nudges downhill lead toward a local minimum, which binary activations would not allow.

IHZwWFHWa-w.q: What happens when the trained network is shown an image of random noise?
options: It leaves all ten output neurons dark because no digit pattern is present
It confidently gives a nonsense answer, as if the noise were a real digit
It lights up all ten output neurons evenly since every digit is equally likely
It refuses to classify the image and flags it as not being a digit
IHZwWFHWa-w.why: Its cost function never rewarded uncertainty, so it is as confident about noise being a five as it is about a real five.

Ilg3gGewQ5U.q: To raise the digit 2 neuron's activation, which incoming weights have the biggest effect?
options: Weights from the dimmest, least active neurons in the layer just before it
Weights connected to the output neurons for other digits
Weights from the brightest, most active neurons in the previous layer
All weights have exactly the same effect
Ilg3gGewQ5U.why: Each weight is multiplied by the previous neuron's activation, so weights from bright neurons change the weighted sum, and the cost, the most.

Ilg3gGewQ5U.q: Why do networks usually train on random mini batches instead of every training example per step?
options: Each step is far cheaper, and a mini batch still approximates the true gradient well
Mini batches give the exact gradient of the full cost function
Using all the examples at once would make the network classify everything as one digit
Mini batches remove the need for backpropagation
Ilg3gGewQ5U.why: Averaging over all data each step is very slow. A mini batch gives a good approximation of the gradient and a big speedup, which is stochastic gradient descent.

tIeHLnjs5U8.q: The derivative of the cost with respect to the last activation is 2 times (aL minus y). What does that tell you?
options: The cost barely changes when the output is far from the desired value
Its size grows with the gap between the output and the desired value
It depends only on the bias, not on the output
It is always equal to the previous neuron's activation
tIeHLnjs5U8.why: The term 2(aL minus y) is proportional to how far the output is from what we want, so a very wrong output means small changes have a big effect on the cost.

tIeHLnjs5U8.q: With many neurons per layer, why is the cost's sensitivity to a neuron in layer L minus 1 a sum?
options: Because each weight is counted twice in the weight matrix, once forward and once backward
Because the biases of every layer must be added together before taking the derivative
Because that neuron affects the cost through several paths, one per neuron in the next layer
Because the cost averages over every training example, and each example adds a term
tIeHLnjs5U8.why: That neuron influences aL0, aL1 and so on, and each of those feeds the cost, so you add up the effects along every path.

VMj-3S1tku0.q: After backpropagation, a.grad is 138. What does that tell you?
options: a will change by 138 on the next update
g is 138 times larger than a
If a is nudged up slightly, g rises with a slope of 138
a contributes 138 percent of the final value of the output g
VMj-3S1tku0.why: A gradient is a slope: it says how g responds when a is tweaked a tiny amount in the positive direction.

VMj-3S1tku0.q: With d = a*b + c, a = 2, b = -3 and c = 10, why does bumping a up slightly make d go down?
options: Because c is positive and large enough to dominate the whole sum
Because the derivative of d with respect to a is b, which is -3
Because the step size h is too small to measure a real change
Because a is smaller than c, so raising it pulls d toward zero
VMj-3S1tku0.why: Differentiating a*b + c with respect to a gives b. Since b is -3, increasing a lowers d at a slope of -3.

VMj-3S1tku0.q: During backpropagation, what does a plus node do with the gradient coming into it?
options: It passes the same gradient unchanged to each of its inputs
It splits the gradient in half between its inputs
It multiplies the gradient by the value of the other input node
It sets its inputs' gradients to zero
VMj-3S1tku0.why: The local derivative of a sum with respect to each input is 1, so by the chain rule the incoming gradient is simply routed to every input.

VMj-3S1tku0.q: In the neuron example, why is the gradient on weight w2 zero?
options: Because w2 was initialized to zero, so it has no effect on the neuron yet
Because tanh squashed the output to zero, which zeroes every gradient below it
Because the plus node blocked the gradient before it could reach that weight
Because its input x2 is zero, so changing w2 does not change the output
VMj-3S1tku0.why: For a times node the local derivative of w2 is the other factor, x2. With x2 equal to 0, wiggling w2 has no effect on the output.

VMj-3S1tku0.q: Why did b = a + a first give a.grad of 1 instead of 2, and how was it fixed?
options: The forward pass computed b wrong; it was fixed by calling backward a second time
The second gradient overwrote the first; it was fixed by accumulating gradients with +=
Topological sort skipped one copy of a; it was fixed by sorting the graph again
The step size was too large for a; it was fixed by lowering the learning rate
VMj-3S1tku0.why: When a value is used more than once, each use contributes a gradient. Setting grad with = overwrote one contribution, so the fix is to add them with +=.

VMj-3S1tku0.q: When tanh was rebuilt from exp, division and other smaller operations, what happened to the gradients on the leaf nodes?
options: They came out identical to the single tanh node
They doubled because the graph was larger
They all became zero because exp has no simple derivative
They matched only after rescaling
VMj-3S1tku0.why: The composed expression is mathematically equal to tanh, so the forward and backward passes match. The level of abstraction is up to you as long as each piece has a local derivative.

VMj-3S1tku0.q: In the gradient descent update, why is the step taken as minus the learning rate times p.grad?
options: Because gradients are always positive, so the minus sign is needed to shrink weights
Because the minus sign keeps every weight between -1 and 1 during training
Because the gradient points toward increasing loss, and we want the loss to go down
Because PyTorch requires negative updates whenever it steps the parameters
VMj-3S1tku0.why: The gradient points in the direction that increases the loss. To minimize the loss, each parameter moves the opposite way.

VMj-3S1tku0.q: What bug did the training loop have, and why did it still seem to work?
options: It used the wrong loss function, but the tiny data set happened to fit anyway
It never called backward, so the weights drifted randomly and still happened to find a low loss
The learning rate decayed to zero too early, but the first few steps were enough
It never zeroed the gradients, so they piled up and acted like a huge step on an easy problem
VMj-3S1tku0.why: Without zeroing grads before backward, each pass adds onto old gradients. On this very simple problem that just acted like a bigger step size.

PaCmpygFfXo.q: Why wrap each word with special start and end tokens before collecting bigrams?
options: To make every word the same length so the bigram counts line up in one table
To capture which characters tend to begin a name and that a name is likely to end
To separate uppercase from lowercase letters before counting the character pairs
To mark and remove duplicate names from the data set before any counting starts
PaCmpygFfXo.why: Plain consecutive pairs miss that E starts Emma and that the word ends after A. The start and end tokens turn those facts into bigrams too.

PaCmpygFfXo.q: Why did he replace the separate start and end tokens with a single dot token?
options: PyTorch cannot index an array larger than 27 by 27, so one of the two tokens had to go
A single token makes sampling deterministic, so every generated name stops at the same place
Nothing followed the end token and nothing came before the start, so a row and a column were all zeros
A dot is required by torch.multinomial, which treats it as the marker for the end of every sample it draws
PaCmpygFfXo.why: With two tokens, the end row and start column were always zero. One dot token used for both roles gives a tidier 27 by 27 array.

PaCmpygFfXo.q: Why are names sampled from the bigram model so poor?
options: The model only looks at the previous character, so it does not know what came earlier in the name
The counts were never normalized into probabilities, so the common letters were sampled far too often
The generator seed was set incorrectly, so each sample drew from the same few rows
The model was trained on only three names, so it had almost no examples to learn from
PaCmpygFfXo.why: When it generates H, it does not know whether H is the first letter or not. It only sees one previous character, so it is a very weak model, though still better than uniform.

PaCmpygFfXo.q: What went wrong when keepdim was removed from P.sum(1) before dividing?
options: The division raised a shape error because a 27 by 27 tensor cannot divide by 27 numbers
The sums were taken over the whole tensor, so every entry was divided by one grand total
The counts were treated as integers in the division and rounded down to zero
The 27 sums were broadcast as a row vector, so the columns were normalized instead of the rows
PaCmpygFfXo.why: Without keepdim the shape is 27. Broadcasting aligns on the right and adds a dimension on the left, making it 1 by 27, which is copied down and divides each column.

PaCmpygFfXo.q: Why use the negative log likelihood as the loss instead of the likelihood itself?
options: It is a sum instead of a product of tiny numbers, and lower values mean a better model
It makes every probability equal to one, so the loss is easy to compare across models
It removes the need to normalize the counts, since the log handles all the scaling
It is the only loss PyTorch can backpropagate through when the outputs are probabilities
PaCmpygFfXo.why: The likelihood is a product of numbers below one and gets very tiny. The log turns it into a sum, and negating it gives a loss where 0 is best and higher is worse.

PaCmpygFfXo.q: Why are the character indices one-hot encoded before going into the neural net?
options: One-hot vectors take less memory than integers, so the forward pass runs much faster
PyTorch tensors cannot hold integers, so each index has to be turned into a float vector first
Neurons multiply inputs by weights, so a raw integer index makes no sense as an input value
One-hot encoding sorts the characters alphabetically so the weight rows stay in order
PaCmpygFfXo.why: An index like 13 is a label, not a quantity to scale by weights. One-hot turns it into a vector of zeros with a single one, which can feed into the layer.

PaCmpygFfXo.q: What does the softmax step do with the 27 outputs of the linear layer?
options: It rounds the logits to the nearest integer counts so they match the bigram table
It exponentiates the logits into positive counts and normalizes each row to sum to one
It picks the single largest output as the next character and discards the other 26
It squares the logits so negative values disappear, then divides by the largest one
PaCmpygFfXo.why: The outputs are read as log counts, or logits. Exponentiating makes them positive like counts, and dividing by the row sum turns them into a probability distribution.

PaCmpygFfXo.q: How does adding a penalty on the squared weights relate to the counting model?
options: Like smoothing, pushing W toward zero makes predictions more uniform, like adding fake counts
It speeds up training by shrinking the gradients, without changing the final predictions
It forces the model to memorize every bigram exactly, just as the count table does
It replaces the negative log likelihood, so the model only learns to keep its weights small
PaCmpygFfXo.why: When all weights are zero, logits are zero and probabilities are uniform. A stronger regularization pull toward zero matches adding more fake counts in the counting approach.

wjZofJX0v4M.q: How does the multi-layer perceptron step differ from the attention block?
options: The vectors do not talk to each other and each goes through the same operation in parallel
It decides which words are relevant to updating the meaning of which other words
It turns the last vector in the sequence into a probability distribution over every possible token
It breaks the input text into tokens and looks up an embedding vector for each one
wjZofJX0v4M.why: Attention lets vectors pass information back and forth. In the perceptron block, each vector is processed on its own, like answering a list of questions about it.

wjZofJX0v4M.q: What is the difference between a model's weights and the data being processed?
options: Weights change with every new prompt, while the data stays fixed after training ends
Weights are learned in training and set behavior, while data encodes the input for one run
Weights are the input tokens, while the data is the probability distribution the model outputs
There is no real difference, since both are just matrices multiplied in the same way
wjZofJX0v4M.why: The weights are the actual brains learned in training. The data is just whatever input, like a text snippet, is fed in for a given run.

wjZofJX0v4M.q: Why did early chatbots seem to lose the thread in long conversations?
options: Their embeddings had too few dimensions to store the meaning of a long conversation
Their temperature was set too high, so the replies drifted further from the topic
Their context size limits how much text they can use when predicting the next word
Their unembedding matrix was too small to cover the words used earlier in the chat
wjZofJX0v4M.why: The network processes a fixed number of vectors at a time, 2048 for GPT-3, so text beyond that window cannot inform the prediction.

wjZofJX0v4M.q: What happens when you raise the temperature in softmax?
options: All weight goes to the single most likely token, so the output becomes predictable
The outputs no longer add up to one, so they must be normalized a second time
The model draws from a larger vocabulary that includes rarer tokens
Lower values get more weight, so the distribution becomes more uniform
wjZofJX0v4M.why: A larger T flattens the distribution so less likely words get picked more often. A smaller T lets the biggest values dominate.

eMlx5fFNoYc.q: After the first step of a transformer, why is the vector for "mole" the same in "one mole of carbon dioxide" and "take a biopsy of the mole"?
options: Because both phrases are too short for attention to change any of the vectors
Because the word has only one meaning in the training data, so it gets one vector
Because the initial embedding is a lookup table with no reference to context
Because the model has not been trained yet, so every word starts out the same
eMlx5fFNoYc.why: The first step just looks up a vector for each token. Only later steps, like attention, let surrounding words pass information in.

eMlx5fFNoYc.q: Why are the entries where later tokens would influence earlier ones set to negative infinity before softmax?
options: So they become zero after softmax while each column still sums to one
So the model pays extra attention to the most recent token in the sequence
So the attention pattern takes less memory
So the dot products stay numerically stable
eMlx5fFNoYc.why: Setting them to zero directly would break normalization. Negative infinity turns into zero after softmax and keeps the columns normalized, which stops later words from giving away the answer.

eMlx5fFNoYc.q: How does a single attention head actually update the embedding of a word like "creature"?
options: It replaces the embedding with the embedding of the most relevant adjective before it
It adds a sum of value vectors, weighted by the attention pattern, to the original embedding
It multiplies the embedding by the query matrix and passes the result to the next layer
It averages the key vectors of all previous words and stores that as the new embedding
eMlx5fFNoYc.why: Each value vector is scaled by its weight in that column, the results are summed into a change, and that change is added to the original embedding.

eMlx5fFNoYc.q: What is the point of running many attention heads in parallel?
options: To make each head's attention pattern smaller so the whole layer uses less memory
To remove the need for masking, since each head only looks at earlier tokens
To let the model use a longer context window by splitting it across the heads
To give the model capacity to learn many distinct ways context changes meaning
eMlx5fFNoYc.why: Each head has its own key, query and value maps, so different heads can capture different kinds of contextual updates, and their proposed changes are summed.

kCc8FmEb1nY.q: What tradeoff does choosing a tokenizer's vocabulary size involve?
options: A larger vocabulary gives longer sequences but a simpler encoder
A smaller vocabulary makes the model bigger but trains it faster
Small vocabularies give long sequences; large ones give short sequences
Subword vocabularies drop rare characters, so they can't round trip text
kCc8FmEb1nY.why: You trade code book size against sequence length. The character tokenizer has 65 tokens and long sequences, while GPT-2's roughly 50,000 tokens encode the same text in far fewer integers.

kCc8FmEb1nY.q: Why train on every context length from 1 up to block size in each chunk?
options: So the model can predict well from as little as one character at sampling time
So the batch dimension can be dropped, since each chunk becomes its own full batch
So the model can read past block size at inference without being truncated
So validation loss and training loss are computed on exactly the same data
kCc8FmEb1nY.why: Karpathy says it isn't only for efficiency: it gets the Transformer used to every context size, so generation can start from a single character. Past block size the context must be truncated.

kCc8FmEb1nY.q: Why does generate feed the whole context to the bigram model, even though it uses only the last token?
options: The bigram model averages all previous tokens before it predicts the next
PyTorch's embedding layer fails when it gets only a single token as input
Feeding everything lowers the loss, since more context improves sampling
So the same function still works later, once the model uses the history
kCc8FmEb1nY.why: Right now the history is ignored, so it looks silly. He keeps generate fixed so it works unchanged when later models actually look further back in the sequence.

kCc8FmEb1nY.q: What does multiplying by a row-normalized lower triangular matrix do to the rows of B?
options: Each output row becomes the sum of all later rows of B, then is normalized
Each output row is the average of B's rows up to and including that position
It sorts B's rows so the largest values end up at the bottom of the matrix
It zeroes out every row except the first, so only the first token is kept
kCc8FmEb1nY.why: The ones in each row of the lower triangle pick out the current and earlier rows, and normalizing each row to sum to one turns the sum into a running average.

kCc8FmEb1nY.q: In self attention, how does a token decide how much to take from another token?
options: It averages all past tokens equally, with weights fixed before training
Its query is dotted with the other token's key, and a match means high affinity
It compares raw embeddings directly, so tokens with the same letters attend more
Its value vector is dotted with each key, and the largest match is copied over
kCc8FmEb1nY.why: Each token emits a query (what am I looking for) and a key (what do I contain). The dot product of query and key sets the data dependent affinity.

kCc8FmEb1nY.q: Why do the attention scores get scaled by one over the square root of head size?
options: To make the attention weights sum to one without needing a softmax step
To shrink the value vectors so the head output matches the embedding size
To stop future tokens from leaking in, together with the triangular mask
To keep variance near one so softmax stays diffuse instead of one-hot
kCc8FmEb1nY.why: Without scaling the variance of the scores grows with head size, and large values make softmax sharpen toward the max, so each node would aggregate from just one other node at initialization.

kCc8FmEb1nY.q: Why do residual connections help a deep Transformer optimize?
options: Addition passes gradients straight through, a highway from loss to input
They normalize each token's features, so the activations never explode
They randomly drop blocks during training, which acts as regularization
They let each block see future tokens, which gives more training signal per step
kCc8FmEb1nY.why: Addition distributes gradients equally to its branches, so gradients flow unimpeded from the supervision to the input, and the residual blocks come online over time.

kCc8FmEb1nY.q: Why is the Transformer built in this video decoder only, with no encoder?
options: Encoders only work with subword tokens, not with character-level tokens
Cross attention needs more GPU memory than the A100 used for training
The text isn't conditioned on any input to encode; it just imitates a file
The triangular mask can only be used when an encoder supplies the keys
kCc8FmEb1nY.why: The original paper needed an encoder to read the French sentence for translation. Here there is nothing to condition on, so like GPT it only needs the masked decoder.

zduSFxRajkE.q: Why does non-English text tend to work worse with these tokenizers?
options: The tokenizer refuses characters outside ASCII and drops them before training
Non-English text is split into more, smaller tokens, so it uses up the context faster
Non-English words are always mapped to the unknown token, so their meaning is lost
The embedding table has no rows for non-English tokens, so they all share one vector
zduSFxRajkE.why: The tokenizer is trained on mostly English, so English gets long tokens while other languages break into many pieces, stretching sequences and filling the context.

zduSFxRajkE.q: Why not just feed the raw UTF-8 bytes into the model as tokens?
options: A 256-token vocabulary makes sequences very long, which wastes the limited context
UTF-8 bytes cannot represent emoji or characters outside the Latin alphabet
Bytes cannot be looked up in an embedding table, since they are not whole words
UTF-8 changes every time the Unicode standard updates, so the model would break
zduSFxRajkE.why: With only 256 possible tokens, text stretches into very long byte sequences, and attention can only cover a finite context, so the model sees less text.

zduSFxRajkE.q: If the tokenizer's training set includes a lot of Japanese text, what is the effect?
options: The language model learns Japanese grammar faster, even with the same token count
Japanese characters are removed from the vocabulary to make room for the new merges
Japanese text falls back to raw bytes more often, so its sequences get longer
More Japanese merges are learned, so Japanese text becomes shorter token sequences
zduSFxRajkE.why: The tokenizer is trained separately. More of a language in its training set means more merges for it, giving denser, shorter sequences for that language.

zduSFxRajkE.q: What is the purpose of GPT-2's regex split before running byte pair encoding?
options: To remove punctuation and extra spaces from the text before any merging starts
To make the text lowercase so the same word always merges the same way
To stop merges across categories like letters, numbers and punctuation
To speed up decoding of the final tokens back into readable text
zduSFxRajkE.why: The text is split into chunks and each chunk is tokenized on its own, so BPE can never merge across chunk boundaries, such as an e with a following space.

zduSFxRajkE.q: What is the end of text token in GPT-2 used for?
options: It marks the boundary between documents in the training data
It marks where a word is split into two tokens
It stands in for any byte sequence that is not valid UTF-8 text
It pads short sequences to the full context length
zduSFxRajkE.why: It is inserted between documents to signal that a document ended and what follows is unrelated. It is the 50,257th token, added on top of the 256 bytes and 50,000 merges.

zduSFxRajkE.q: In SentencePiece, what happens to a rare code point like an unseen Korean character when byte fallback is turned off?
options: It is encoded as its UTF-8 bytes
It becomes the unknown token
It is merged with the nearest common character
It is dropped from the text silently
zduSFxRajkE.why: Without byte fallback, code points not in the vocabulary all map to the unknown token, which is why Llama turned byte fallback on.

zduSFxRajkE.q: Which is a reason not to make the vocabulary size extremely large?
options: Sequences would get longer, so each prompt fills the context window faster than before
The embedding table would have to shrink to fit the extra tokens in memory
The tokenizer could no longer decode text back into the original bytes
Each token appears more rarely in training, so its embedding may be undertrained
zduSFxRajkE.why: With a huge vocabulary, each token shows up less often, so its vectors get few updates. The embedding table and output layer also grow, adding compute.

zduSFxRajkE.q: Why did prompts containing SolidGoldMagikarp make GPT models behave strangely?
options: The string was on a list of banned words, so the safety filter garbled the model's reply
The string was too long to fit in the context, so the prompt was cut off partway through the text
It had its own token, but that token never appeared in training, so its embedding was untrained
The token was confused with the end of text token, so the model stopped or rambled oddly
zduSFxRajkE.why: The Reddit username was common in the tokenizer's training data but absent from the language model's data, so its embedding row was never updated and acts like unallocated memory.

l8pRSuU81PU.q: How does the video describe the different jobs of attention and the MLP inside a Transformer block?
options: Attention runs on each token alone (a map), while the MLP mixes information across all of the tokens (a reduce)
Attention lets tokens exchange information (a reduce), while the MLP works on each token individually (a map)
Both attention and the MLP mix information across all tokens in the sequence
Attention normalizes the residual stream, while the MLP adds the position information
l8pRSuU81PU.why: Attention is the communication step, a weighted sum across tokens. The MLP runs on every token separately, so a block is a repeated map and reduce.

l8pRSuU81PU.q: Why is a starting loss of about 11 a good sign for the randomly initialized model?
options: It shows the model has already memorized the first batch of training tokens
It means the learning rate is set correctly for AdamW at the start of training
It proves the GPT-2 weights were loaded correctly from Hugging Face before training began
It is close to negative ln(1/50257), about 10.82, so the predictions are roughly uniform
l8pRSuU81PU.why: With 50257 tokens, a uniform guess gives a loss of negative ln(1/50257), about 10.82. A loss near that means the network is not confidently wrong at the start.

l8pRSuU81PU.q: Why does GPT-2 share one weight matrix between the token embedding and the output classifier?
options: Similar tokens should get similar embeddings and outputs, and sharing saves about 30% of the parameters
The output layer cannot be trained unless it reuses the embedding gradients directly at each step
Sharing the matrix lets the model use a longer context window than its usual 1024 tokens
PyTorch requires the embedding and the final linear layer to point to the same tensor in memory
l8pRSuU81PU.why: Both ends of the network want semantically similar tokens to behave alike, so the weights are tied. The 768 by 50257 matrix is about 40 million of the 124 million parameters.

l8pRSuU81PU.q: Why does training in bfloat16 not need the gradient scalers that fp16 training needs?
options: bfloat16 keeps more mantissa bits than fp16, so even very small gradients are stored exactly
bfloat16 stores weights in float32 and keeps only the gradients in 16 bits, so nothing underflows
bfloat16 keeps the same exponent bits as fp32, so it has the full range and only loses precision
bfloat16 runs only in the forward pass, so the gradients never leave float32 at all
l8pRSuU81PU.why: bfloat16 truncates the mantissa but keeps the 8 exponent bits, so it covers the same range as fp32. fp16 reduced the range, which is why it needed gradient scaling.

l8pRSuU81PU.q: Flash attention does more floating point operations than the plain attention code. Why is it still much faster?
options: It skips the exact softmax and uses a cheaper approximation of attention that needs fewer reads
It never writes the large T by T attention matrix to high bandwidth memory, so it avoids slow memory traffic
It runs attention in int8, which the tensor cores can process about eight times faster than they process bfloat16
It drops the causal mask, so each token does less work when it attends to the earlier tokens
l8pRSuU81PU.why: The cost is in reads and writes to HBM, not in FLOPs. Using the online softmax trick, flash attention keeps the work on chip and never materializes the attention matrix.

l8pRSuU81PU.q: When accumulating gradients over several micro steps, why must each micro step's loss be divided by the number of steps?
options: Otherwise the learning rate warmup would end too early, since each micro step counts as one step
Otherwise the summed gradients would overflow in bfloat16 and turn into infinity
Otherwise the loss would be averaged twice, once per micro batch and once by the optimizer
Repeated backward calls sum the gradients, so dividing restores the mean over the full batch
l8pRSuU81PU.why: Each backward call adds to the gradients, which acts like a sum of losses. Dividing by the accumulation steps puts back the missing normalizer, so the result matches one big batch.

l8pRSuU81PU.q: With DDP and gradient accumulation, why does the video turn on gradient sync only on the last micro step?
options: Syncing on every micro step wastes communication, since gradients can add up locally and be averaged once
Syncing early would make every GPU train on the same data shard instead of its own slice
DDP can only average gradients once per training run, so it has to wait for the final step
The first micro steps produce no gradients yet, so there is nothing to send between the GPUs until the end
l8pRSuU81PU.why: The all reduce that averages gradients across GPUs is costly. Gradients are accumulated locally across micro steps, then averaged once on the final backward pass.

l8pRSuU81PU.q: How does the video score its small model on HellaSwag?
options: It shows all four endings in one prompt and asks the model to output the letter A, B, C or D
It picks the option whose text is the shortest after the shared context
It picks the completion whose tokens get the lowest average loss after the shared context
It fine tunes the model on HellaSwag examples and reports training accuracy
l8pRSuU81PU.why: Models this small cannot handle a multiple choice format, so each option is scored as a plain token completion and the most likely one wins.

SQ3fZ1sAqXI.q: Why might optimizing attention in a small model be wasted effort at frontier scale?
options: Large models drop attention layers and use only MLP layers instead
At large scale MLP flops dominate, so attention's share gets washed out
Attention flops grow so fast at scale that no kernel optimization can keep up
Small models run attention on the CPU, while large models use the GPU
SQ3fZ1sAqXI.why: In small models attention and MLP flops are roughly comparable, but at 175 billion parameters the MLPs dominate. Tuning attention at small scale can mean optimizing the wrong thing.

SQ3fZ1sAqXI.q: What does Percy say is the right reading of the bitter lesson?
options: Scale is all that matters, so algorithm work is no longer worth doing
Clever algorithms matter more than scale, so small models are enough
Hand-built features beat learning once a model gets large enough
Algorithms at scale matter, and efficiency counts more at large scale
SQ3fZ1sAqXI.why: He rejects the idea that only capital matters. Accuracy is a product of efficiency and resources, and when a run costs hundreds of millions of dollars you can't afford waste.

SQ3fZ1sAqXI.q: According to Percy, what should you try before training a language model from scratch?
options: Prompting or fine-tuning an existing model, if that already works
Building your own tokenizer, since that drives most of the quality
Scraping a fresh Common Crawl dump so the data is your own from day one
Writing custom Triton kernels so your first training run is efficient
SQ3fZ1sAqXI.why: He says prompting and fine-tuning are great, and if they work you should start there. Training from scratch is not the right first step for every problem.

SQ3fZ1sAqXI.q: What is the main bottleneck the kernels unit tries to reduce on a GPU?
options: The number of floating point units, which limits each matrix multiply
The time spent compiling Python code into GPU instructions for each step
Moving data between off-chip memory and compute, the warehouse to factory trip
The size of the L1 cache, which caps how many parameters a model can hold
SQ3fZ1sAqXI.why: Memory is the warehouse and compute is the factory, and the big cost is data movement between them. Techniques like fusion and tiling cut that movement.

SQ3fZ1sAqXI.q: What does the Chinchilla rule of thumb leave out, by Percy's account?
options: The cost of data cleaning, since it assumes all tokens are high quality
The number of GPUs, since it assumes training runs on a single device
The choice of optimizer, since it assumes plain SGD for every model size
Inference cost, since it only asks for the best model for a training budget
SQ3fZ1sAqXI.why: The rule of about 20 tokens per parameter finds the best model for a given training compute budget. It doesn't account for what the model will cost to serve.

SQ3fZ1sAqXI.q: Why does the class train for just a single epoch over the data?
options: It is compute constrained with plenty of data, so seeing new data beats repeats
It is data constrained, so a second pass would only memorize the same few tokens
A second epoch breaks the tokenizer, which was trained on the first pass only
The scaling laws in assignment three are only valid for single-epoch runs
SQ3fZ1sAqXI.why: In the current GPU-poor regime there is a lot of data but little compute, so it's more efficient to see more data than to revisit any one example. Data constrained labs may change that.

SQ3fZ1sAqXI.q: What is the main problem with byte-based tokenization?
options: The vocabulary is huge, since every Unicode code point needs its own slot
It can't round trip, since some characters can't be decoded from bytes
Sequences get long, and attention cost grows quadratically with length
Rare words fall back to an unknown token, which breaks the perplexity
SQ3fZ1sAqXI.why: With a compression ratio of one byte per token, sequences are very long, and naive attention is quadratic in sequence length, which is terrible for efficiency.

SQ3fZ1sAqXI.q: How does BPE decide which sequences get their own token?
options: It splits text with a regex and gives each whole word its own token
It repeatedly merges the most frequent adjacent pair into a new token
It assigns tokens by Unicode code point and merges only rare characters
It picks the tokens that minimize the model's loss after a short run
SQ3fZ1sAqXI.why: BPE starts from bytes and keeps merging the most common pair of adjacent tokens, so common sequences become one token and rare ones stay as several.

61yRuOMSfMc.q: When a model fits entirely on the GPU, what mainly limits prefill speed versus decode speed?
options: Prefill is limited by storage speed, decode by CPU threads
Both are limited only by how much VRAM the card has
Prefill is limited by memory bandwidth (GB/s), decode by compute (FLOPs)
Prefill is limited by compute (FLOPs), decode by memory bandwidth
61yRuOMSfMc.why: Prefill processes the whole prompt at once and is compute bound. Decode reads the weights for every token, so memory bandwidth sets its ceiling.

61yRuOMSfMc.q: Why does the DGX Spark run models slower than a 3090 yet hold far more memory?
options: It uses LPDDR memory, which is cheaper and cooler but has much lower bandwidth than GDDR or HBM
It has no discrete GPU, so all the math in each layer runs on its ARM CPU cores instead
Its memory is faster than a 3090's, but its software stack is far less optimized for inference
It stores the model weights on NVMe storage and streams them in, instead of keeping them in memory
61yRuOMSfMc.why: High bandwidth GDDR and HBM are hard to produce and need cooling. The Spark's LPDDR runs at about 273 GB per second, roughly a quarter of a 3090, but is cheap enough to fit 128 GB.

61yRuOMSfMc.q: What is the drawback of pipeline parallelism when a model is split across two machines?
options: It requires both machines to hold a full copy of the model weights in memory
It only works with models smaller than one machine's memory, which defeats the purpose
Each stage waits for the stage before it, so it is not the fastest way to split
It prevents a mixture of experts model from using more than one expert at a time
61yRuOMSfMc.why: In pipeline parallelism each group of GPUs is a stage, and a stage must wait for the previous one, so splitting the model half and half or arranging experts is often faster.

K75j8MkwgJ0.q: Why do K quants (the models tagged with K) do better than plain Q4 quantization?
options: They store every number at full 32 bit precision, so nothing is lost in the conversion
They give small numbers and big numbers their own suitably sized slots instead of one rigid set
They remove half of the model's parameters entirely, so the rest can use more bits each
They move the model's numbers from RAM onto the hard drive and load only what is needed
K75j8MkwgJ0.why: Plain Q4 forces every value into the same 16 slots. K quants use separate areas so groups of small numbers get precise slots and big numbers get fitting space.
